content: Arsphenamine is a pharmaceutical agent that was historically employed in the treatment of syphilis and trypanosomiasis. It holds the distinction of being the first modern chemotherapeutic drug. In 1908, Sahachiro Hata discovered the anti-syphilitic properties of this compound while working in Paul Ehrlich's laboratory. This discovery was part of a systematic investigation of hundreds of newly synthesized organic arsenical compounds. Ehrlich had hypothesized that by screening a large number of chemical compounds, it would be possible to identify a drug with antimicrobial activity. His team initiated a methodical search for such a magic bullet among derivatives of atoxyl, a highly toxic arsenical compound. This effort marked the first organized attempt to optimize the biological activity of a lead compound through systematic chemical modifications, laying the foundation for modern pharmaceutical research. Arsphenamine was introduced to the market in 1910 under the trade name Salvarsan. It was also referred to as 606 because it was the 606th compound synthesized and tested during the research process. Salvarsan represented a significant advancement over the previously used inorganic mercury compounds for syphilis treatment, as it was the first organic anti-syphilitic agent. In 1912, a more water-soluble but slightly less effective arsenical compound, Neosalvarsan (also known as neoarsphenamine), became available. However, both Salvarsan and Neosalvarsan carried substantial risks of side effects. By the 1940s, these arsenical compounds were replaced by penicillin as the standard treatment for syphilis. The causative agent of syphilis is a spirochete bacterium known as Treponema pallidum. Arsphenamine itself is not directly toxic to spirochetes; it requires metabolic activation within the body to convert into its active form. This characteristic underscores the importance of Hata's animal testing in the discovery of the drug. After leaving Ehrlich's laboratory, Hata continued his research on this new medicine in Japan. Regarding its chemical structure, arsphenamine was initially believed to contain an arsenic-arsenic (As=As) double bond. However, in 2005, it was revealed that the compound is actually a mixture of a cyclic trimer and a pentamer. The revised structural model indicates that arsphenamine features single As-As bonds rather than double bonds.
